sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:

【Introduction · p0025】Food fraud, adulteration, counterfeiting, and food criminality are concepts often seen in dialogues around global food safety. Entities such as the Global Food Safety Initiative (GFSI), the Grocery Manufacturers Association (GMA) in the United States, the US Pharmacopeia (USP), and European Parliament reports characterize food fraud as the deliberate and deceptive misrepresentation of food for monetary profit (Spink et al., 2019). Food fraud encompasses more than economically driven adulteration; it often involves deception, including counterfeiting, as well as adulteration, and may also include fraud, tampering, diversion, tax evasion, grey market operations, and overflow goods. Recent crises in the food business have intensified the problem of food fraud, amplifying the necessity to combat fraud across supply chains. Regrettably, existing food safety management methods are not explicitly tailored to address or alleviate fraud (Rizzuti, 2021).

【Introduction · p0030】Considering the deliberate nature of food fraud, strategies for addressing food safety must be reformed to prioritize fraud prevention and vulnerability mitigation, rather than only maintaining safety. Fraud vulnerability is a weakness or a flaw that enables negative events in a system. However, research exploring the antecedent factors that lead to the occurrence of food fraud vulnerability is scarce, whereas the existing data, therefore, draws its understanding fundamentally from other corporate crimes (Wang et al., 2024). Given the complexity of food fraud problems, it is necessary to examine the factors that spur fraudulent activities and the main factors that would make a food product more vulnerable.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:

【Limitations of conventional detection methods · p0200】The traditional method of food testing, although used for a long time and evolved with technological advancements, is still facing a lot of heat from the rising demand for food safety in recent times. Most chromatographic techniques, such as high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and gas chromatography (GC), require vary sophisticated equipment's with trained personnel's and often require complex sample preparation and operation, which can be expensive and time-consuming for the food manufacturers (He, Bai, et al., 2020b, 2020c; He, Joseph, et al., 2020). Some compounds in food products have poor electrochemical activity, which necessitates additional precolumn derivatization so as to make them detectable, which further complicates the problem (Cuadros-Rodríguez et al., 2021). One major limitation also comes with the standardization of methods, as most food testing operations lack official standardized chromatographic protocols, which limit the scope of chromatographic fingerprinting testing (Sontag et al., 2019).

【Limitations of conventional detection methods · p0210】Although newer methods in Sensory evaluation, like using trained panels and controlled protocols, have overcome the problems of reproducibility, the training costs and overhead costs of hiring a trained assessor make the process complex and costly, which often limits their regular use. Most of the times, the assessors are trained with specialty in one product like wine, tea or apples which makes then highly specific for the industry and lesser known industries have to spend a large sum for finding a suitable person. Also in industries where the sample size is quite large, like in olive oil and agricultural products, there is need for a large number of assessors as most human would get saturated after evaluation of a limited number of products which necessitates the requirement of instrumental analysis to cope up with large volumes of samples (Quintanilla-Casas et al., 2020). To overcome these limitations, devices like e-nose and e-tongue have been developed and improved in sensitivity and selectivity, yet they are still not accurate for complex mixtures or low-concentration compounds, which potentially leads to less accurate results. Unlike the human assessors, the accuracy of these devices is heavily dependent on strict control over sample preparation and data processing, but any deviation in these steps can lead to inconsistent results (Tan & Xu, 2020). Although these methods can prove to be affordable in long terms yet their initial setup costs and maintenances are expensive which limit their use to large institutions only. The complexity of integrating and calibrating the sensors and software for these devices further adds to the complexity for small industries with not much of a highly skilled workforce.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:

【Conclusion and future perspectives · p0690】The reviewed literature provides sufficient information to make conclusion that the main advantage of microfluidic systems does not consist in replacement of laboratory techniques but in the combination with these methods and making rapid screening decisions possible in the places without conventional laboratories. Nevertheless, many applications have been proved only under experimental conditions in the case of specific matrices. Thus, future researches should focus on increasing sensitivity, selectivity, decreasing cross-reactivity, overcoming matrix effects, and proving reproducibility on diverse real-life samples. Multiplexed systems, which can detect several indicators of fraud simultaneously, may become a new trend in this field.

【Conclusion and future perspectives · p0685】Nevertheless, traditional analytic methods such as chromatography, spectroscopy, and DNA analysis are highly valuable for reliable detection of fraud in food. Nonetheless, due to the need for special equipment, skilled personnel, and laboratory conditions, they are not always suitable for rapid on-site detection of food fraud. From the literature review conducted, one can conclude that the value of microfluidics in food fraud detection is based on the possibility of the integration of sample preparation and analysis into a compact, portable, and relatively cheap device. Microfluidic technologies are applied in such areas as adulterant detection, allergen screening, pathogen detection, and food authentication.
